metadata.title: MS NOW, CNN and Politico say their journalists were denied access to White House after Trump ban

sources.text:
The media outlets Donald Trump banned from the White House have responded to his order.
The U.S. president announced the ban in a Truth Social post earlier in the week and promised to extend it to other outlets he accuses of spreading fake news. The move marks the latest escalation in his long-running battle with the press, which also includes several defamation lawsuits.
CNN Calls Trump’s White House Ban An ‘Illegal Assault’
After Trump banned several media outlets from the White House, CNN, one of the affected organizations, quickly released a statement supporting its White House team and reaffirming its commitment to covering the administration.
The network described the potential ban as an “illegal assault” on constitutionally protected press freedoms and argued that the Trump administration had no right to impose it.
CNN did not recall its staff from the White House, and its reporters were still seen on the grounds Friday afternoon. A CNN crew was also still traveling with Vice President JD Vance.
Politico Vows To Defend Its First Amendment Rights
Politico, another outlet named in Trump’s ban, released a similar statement.
In a statement to The Hill, Politico said it would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones.” The outlet also pledged to “vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them.”
Meanwhile, MS NOW, the network formerly known as MSNBC, initially declined to issue a formal statement on the ban. However, host Nicolle Wallace weighed in with a scathing assessment during the program “Deadline: White House.”
“In terms of the press, there is the First Amendment that protects our right to do this, but someone in the White House knows this even if Trump doesn’t. The intention is to intimidate, to chill, to sand the edges off, and to make people afraid of doing their jobs,” she said.

- Noah Kahan blasted Trump’s White House for using his music in a social media post.
- Comedian Galifianakis slammed comedians who “suck up” to the president.

- Trump’s team lashed out at a “sick, deluded freak” reporter over a Natalie Harp Ireland post.
- Trump threw a tantrum over the Nobel Peace Prize and “lied again” in the Oval Office.
WHCA Says Press Freedom Does Not Depend On Trump’s Approval
Trump’s ban also drew condemnation from the White House Correspondents’ Association.
According to the association’s president, Jacqui Heinrich, the Constitution protects press freedom from government interference. That protection “does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask.”
She added that the dispute was “about more than the rights of journalists.” It also concerned the American people’s right “to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.”
The WHCA, she said, remains “in defense of our colleagues at CNN, MSNOW, and Politico who are being singled out for doing their jobs.”
Trump Accuses Banned Outlets Of Reporting ‘Fiction And Lies’
Trump announced the ban on his Truth Social account, where he has frequently posted scathing attacks on media outlets amid his feud with the press.
“Media outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president said after announcing the ban.
At the time, he also signaled that more bans could follow, writing, “fake news media outlets to follow,” although he did not name the other outlets he was referring to.
Donald Trump Doubles Down On Media Ban: ‘You Get Sick Of It’
Trump defended the ban during an Oval Office event focused on health care on Friday afternoon.
He told reporters there was no particular reason for the timing, saying, “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it.” He also threatened to ban more outlets in the future.
Asked whether the move was likely to survive a legal challenge, he responded, “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time.”

Senior White House staffers learned of President Donald Trump’s media ban at the same time as the general public, according to a new report from Politico.
Trump issued a directive banning reporters from CNN, MSNBC, and Politico while Chief of Staff Susie Wiles was out of town, sources told Politico.
Many in the West Wing were unaware of the move until they saw the president’s Friday afternoon announcement on his Truth Social platform.
Trump accused the three news organizations of reporting “LIES” but did not point to any specific article as the trigger for his decision.
Sources indicate that Trump had floated the idea of a media ban previously and chose to act on it while his top adviser was not in the building.
Over a dozen current and former Trump officials told Politico they were “puzzled by the development,” with others describing the 80-year-old president’s edict as a “head-scratcher.”
White House security revoked the physical press badges of CNN, MSNBC, and Politico reporters on Saturday, denying them entry to the building upon arrival.
MSNBC’s White House reporter, Akayla Gardner, described the moment her credentials were disabled at the gate.
“I attempted to scan my badge, which we have to do to be able to get into the White House grounds; it did not work,” Gardner said on air. “There was a red beeping light, and so the officer asked me to hand over my badge; he said that it was disabled.”
Sources tell Politico that discussions have taken place about expanding the ban to additional outlets, with Trump suggesting Friday that The New York Times and The Washington Post could be future targets.
Despite pushback from members of his own MAGA base over First Amendment concerns, Trump reportedly intends for the ban to be lasting and binding.
“It’s real and permanent as far as POTUS is concerned,” a source told Politico.
Sources also indicate that Trump has raised the idea of relocating the White House press corps to the adjacent Eisenhower Executive Office Building, which would cut off reporters’ direct access to the West Wing.

A dramatic White House threat issued one day earlier became an enforced reality Saturday morning when journalists arrived for work and discovered that their credentials no longer opened the gates.
The action affected reporters from three major news organizations, transforming an announcement that initially lacked operational details into a direct restriction on access to the presidential complex.
Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied entry to the White House grounds after President Donald Trump declared the outlets banned “effective immediately” over coverage he characterized as “Fake News.”
CNN senior White House reporter Betsy Klein said she attempted to enter Saturday morning and learned that her permanent White House press credential had been deactivated.
A Secret Service agent confiscated Klein’s badge at the entrance and referred her to the White House press office when she asked why her access had been removed.
CNN confirmed the access denial and said its journalists would continue covering the federal government despite efforts to restrict their physical access to government buildings.
“We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government,” CNN said in its statement.
MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Gardner and a network photographer encountered a similar situation when they arrived at the complex Saturday.
Gardner said an officer told her that her badge had been disabled and requested that she surrender it, while explaining that the decision came from above him.
“I asked why I was not able to get inside,” Gardner said during a live report from outside the White House perimeter, adding that the officer responded, “It was above him.”
CNN statement following being denied access to the White House grounds this morning: pic.twitter.com/7Ox03COW0o
— CNN Communications (@CNNPR) September 19, 2026
MS NOW said it intended to take any steps necessary to defend its First Amendment rights and the role of independent journalism.
Politico also confirmed that White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry, completing enforcement against journalists from all three organizations named by Trump.
Trump had announced the ban Friday on Truth Social, accusing the three organizations of repeatedly publishing fiction and lies about him, his administration and the United States.
“Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” Trump wrote after naming CNN, MS NOW and Politico in the announcement.
The president later told reporters that no single article prompted the decision, describing it instead as the result of accumulated coverage over the previous two years.
“You get sick of it,” Trump said, while arguing that media organizations could publish what they wanted but did not have to receive White House access.
Saturday’s confiscated and disabled credentials supplied the clearest answer by preventing named reporters from entering the grounds where they ordinarily work.
The White House referred questions about the restrictions to Trump’s previous remarks rather than offering a separate explanation of the standards used to revoke the credentials.
The affected organizations contend that the government cannot selectively deny established press access because officials object to an outlet’s reporting or editorial viewpoint.
Trump and his defenders maintain that presidents have authority to manage access to limited White House spaces and should not be required to accommodate organizations they consider dishonest.
The dispute is likely to reach federal court, where the central question would be whether the restrictions represent permissible control of access or unconstitutional retaliation based on viewpoint.
Previous disputes involving the White House credentials of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta and Associated Press reporters resulted in court orders restoring at least some access, although the facts and procedural history differed.
For the three organizations targeted Friday, the controversy has now moved beyond a presidential warning: their journalists arrived Saturday and were physically prevented from entering the White House grounds.

“It’s so much bigger than CNN,” Stelter said Saturday. “This is a free speech test in America.”

During the Biden administration, Stelter hosted a discussion about Fox News and its place in the White House press corps.
“Should it be a part of the White House press pool?” Stelter asked during the segment, before questioning whether Fox should be afforded the privileges that come with news gathering.
The resurfaced clip prompted critics to accuse Stelter and other journalists of suddenly discovering a principle they were willing to debate when the network in question was Fox News.
Fox News defended CNN when the Trump White House revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s credential in 2018. Fox News President Jay Wallace said at the time that Secret Service passes for working White House journalists “should never be weaponized,” and Fox joined other news organizations supporting CNN’s legal fight.
Trump announced Friday that CNN, MS NOW and Politico were banned from the White House, accusing the organizations of repeatedly reporting what he called “FAKE NEWS.”
The outlets have condemned the decision and argued that excluding journalists because of their coverage violates constitutional press protections.
The White House Correspondents’ Association also objected. Its president, Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich, said First Amendment protections do not depend on whether a president approves of an outlet’s reporting or questions.

President Donald Trump has announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are being barred from the White House, marking another dramatic turn in his long-running battle with parts of the American news media.
The decision immediately grabbed national attention because it affects three of the country's most recognizable news organizations and raises new questions about access to the president and his administration.
Trump said the outlets would no longer be allowed into the White House because, in his view, they have repeatedly published inaccurate stories about him. He argued that the organizations have spread what he called "fake news" for years and insisted the move was necessary.
The announcement quickly sparked debate across the political and media landscape, with supporters and critics offering very different reactions to the decision.
Why this matters
The dispute is about much more than a disagreement between a president and a few news organizations.
White House access gives reporters the opportunity to attend briefings, ask questions, cover official events and report directly on the decisions made by the country's highest office. Restricting that access naturally draws attention because it affects how information reaches the public.
The latest development also highlights the continuing debate over the balance between presidential authority and freedom of the press. Supporters of Trump's decision argue that no news organization has a guaranteed right to special access if it repeatedly publishes inaccurate reporting.
Critics, however, believe excluding journalists because of their coverage could create concerns about transparency and the public's right to receive information from different sources.
Different reactions emerge
Not surprisingly, the decision prompted an immediate response from the affected organizations.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico defended their journalism and rejected the accusations that their reporting was intentionally false. Each maintained that it would continue covering the White House and the Trump administration despite the new restrictions.
The announcement also drew reactions from press freedom groups, legal analysts and media experts. Many pointed out that disagreements between presidents and journalists are nothing new, but limiting access to certain outlets often leads to wider discussions about constitutional protections and the role of an independent press.
Some legal observers expect the issue could eventually be challenged through the courts if the restrictions remain in place.
Trump's history with the media
Trump's relationship with major news organizations has been tense for many years.
During his first presidential campaign, he frequently criticized television networks and newspapers that he believed treated him unfairly. After entering the White House, those clashes became a regular feature of his presidency, with heated exchanges during press conferences and public appearances.
The phrase "fake news" became one of Trump's most recognizable political expressions. He has repeatedly used it to describe reporting that he believes is inaccurate or misleading.
At the same time, many journalists and media organizations have argued that strong questioning of public officials is a normal part of holding government accountable. That disagreement has remained at the center of Trump's relationship with the press throughout his time in national politics.
A debate that reaches beyond politics
Although the story involves political figures, its impact extends beyond Washington.
The discussion touches on broader issues that affect journalists, government institutions and the public. Access to official events allows reporters to ask questions directly instead of relying solely on prepared statements. Because of that, any decision involving press access usually attracts significant public attention.
Media experts note that conflicts between governments and news organizations have appeared throughout American history under presidents from both political parties. However, each situation is different, and legal questions often depend on the specific actions taken and the reasons behind them.
That is why many observers are closely watching how this latest dispute develops over the coming weeks.
What happens next
For now, the White House decision has added another chapter to Trump's ongoing conflict with several major news organizations.
Whether the restrictions remain in place, are modified or face legal challenges will likely become clearer in the weeks ahead. Lawyers, constitutional scholars and press advocates are expected to examine the decision carefully as more details emerge.
The story is also likely to remain in the spotlight because it combines politics, law and media, three subjects that often generate strong public interest. Any future court filings, official statements or policy changes could shape how the issue unfolds.
Until then, the debate continues over where the line should be drawn between a president's control over White House access and the principles of a free and independent press.
As the discussion continues, both supporters and critics of the decision agree on one point: the outcome could have lasting significance. Whatever happens next may influence future relationships between presidents and the journalists who cover them.
